etymology: From Jesus + freak in its 1960s sense of a devotee or enthusiast ("a jazz freak"; the hippies called themselves "freaks"). Jesus freak appeared around 1969–71 for the converts of the Jesus Movement: long-haired former hippies and drug users who came to Christ through coffeehouses, beach baptisms, Calvary Chapel in Costa Mesa, and street evangelism. Time put "The Jesus Revolution" on its cover on June 21, 1971. The name began as mockery; many converts adopted it as a badge.
biblical_def: A Jesus freak was a convert of the early-1970s Jesus Movement: a hippie who had found Christ and could not stop talking about Him, with long hair, a big Bible, a "One Way" sign, and a zeal that embarrassed his parents’ church. Today the phrase means any intensely, openly devoted Christian. The Christian observation: the world has always thought such people were out of their minds. The Lord Jesus’ own family said, "He is beside himself" (Mar 3:21). Festus told Paul, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Act 26:24). The rulers of Thessalonica complained, "These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also" (Act 17:6). When the council saw Peter and John, "unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus" (Act 4:13). That is the honorable side of the name: Scripture commands a believer to be "fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11), and a cold, respectable Christianity is the stranger thing. But Paul also knew a zeal that goes wrong: "they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom 10:2). Some Jesus freaks burned bright and burned out; some drifted into cults that preyed on their enthusiasm. The lasting fruit came where the zeal was rooted in sound doctrine and a faithful church. Many pastors, missionaries, and Christian parents of today’s grandparent generation were Jesus freaks once. A family can honor that fire and pray that their children catch it — with knowledge.
webster_summary: Early-1970s name, first mocking then embraced, for the zealous converts of the Jesus Movement — the kind of disciple the world has always called "beside himself" (Mar 3:21), whose zeal Scripture commands (Rom 12:11) but wants according to knowledge (Rom 10:2).
webster_full: JESUS FREAK, n. (Boomer slang, c. 1969–71) A convert of the Jesus Movement, typically a former hippie, known for open, fervent devotion to Christ; hence any zealous, outspoken Christian. Often derisive at first; later adopted with pride.

Webster (1828) — ZEALOT, noun Zelot. One who engages warmly in any cause, and pursues his object with earnestness and ardor. It is generally used in dispraise, or applied to one whose ardor in intemperate and censurable. The fury of zealots was one cause of the destruction of Jerusalem.
Decode for families: if Grandpa was a Jesus freak in 1972, ask him to tell you how he came to faith. It will be worth hearing.
scriptures: And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
Mar 3:21
And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself.
Act 17:6
And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also;
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
corruption_summary: The world mocks zeal for Christ as madness, as it always has; Scripture commands fervent spirit but warns that zeal without knowledge can go astray.
corruption_paragraphs: The mockery in the name is the mockery of Festus. The world does not mind religion that stays polite; it minds a young man who has met Jesus and talks about Him at the gas station. The Jesus Movement embarrassed many established churches, which could not decide whether to welcome long-haired converts or require them to cut their hair first. Some churches welcomed them, and grew; others did not, and the converts went elsewhere. The lesson for congregations is permanent: do not quench real zeal because it arrives looking strange.

The other lesson is Paul’s in Rom 10:2. Zeal is a fire; it needs a hearth. Without teaching, accountability, and the ordinary means of grace, the hottest convert can burn out or be captured by a cult — and some in the early 1970s were. The best fruit of the Jesus Movement came where enthusiasm met doctrine: men and women who are still in the pew fifty years later, still fervent, now also wise.
roots_summary: Jesus (Greek Iēsous, Hebrew Yeshua, "the LORD saves") + 1960s freak (devotee) → Jesus freak, c. 1969–71; Time, "The Jesus Revolution," June 21, 1971.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yeshua — "the LORD saves" → Greek Iēsous → Jesus (Mat 1:21)
1960s slang: freak — an enthusiast; the hippies’ name for themselves
c. 1969–71: Jesus freak, Jesus people — converts of the Jesus Movement
June 21, 1971: Time cover, "The Jesus Revolution"
Greek zēlos — zeal (Rom 10:2); zeontes — "fervent" (Rom 12:11)
usage: "Grandpa got saved at a beach baptism in 1971. His dad called him a Jesus freak. Two years later his dad got saved too."
They took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus (Act 4:13).
Fervent in spirit; serving the Lord (Rom 12:11).

etymology: From the Jesus Movement of the early 1970s: the One Way sign — the index finger raised straight up — was the Christian answer to the counterculture’s two-fingered peace sign, declaring that Jesus is the one way to God (Joh 14:6). It appeared on bumper stickers, posters, T-shirts, and buttons, often with an arrow pointing upward, and was flashed by tens of thousands at gatherings such as Explo ’72 in Dallas. The phrase is borrowed from the traffic sign one way.
biblical_def: One Way was the Jesus Movement’s sign: a single finger pointed up, shown to friends, strangers, and passing cars, meaning "Jesus is the only way." In 1971 it was everywhere young Christians gathered. The Christian observation: the sign is a sermon in a gesture, and the sermon is Christ’s own. "Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (Joh 14:6). Peter preached the same before the council: "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Act 4:12). The Lord described the two roads: "wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction ... strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it" (Mat 7:13–14). The counterculture said all paths lead to the top of the mountain; the One Way sign said there is one path, and it is a Person. That claim offended in 1971 and offends more today, when many treat any exclusive claim as arrogance. But it is not arrogance to point to the only bridge over a river; it is love. The sign also has a gentleness worth keeping: it points up, not at anyone. A family can teach the One Way sign to a child with the promise of Isaiah: "thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it" (Isa 30:21).
webster_summary: Jesus Movement sign (early 1970s): the index finger raised to declare that Jesus is the one way to God — Christ’s own claim, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Joh 14:6), against the counterculture’s many paths.
webster_full: ONE WAY, n. / gesture (Jesus Movement, early 1970s; Boomer era) The sign of the raised index finger, signifying that Jesus Christ is the only way to God; also printed as a slogan with an upward arrow.

Webster (1828) — WAY, noun [G., Latin ] 1. Literally, a passing; hence, a passage; the place of passing; hence, a road of any kind; a highway; a private road; a lane; a street; any place for the passing of men; cattle or other animals; a word of very comprehensive signification. 2. Length of space; as a great way; a little way 3. Course; direction of motion or travel. What way did he take? Which way shall I go? Keep in the way of truth and knowledge. Mark what way I make. 4. Passage; room for passing. Make way for the jury.
Decode for families: the Christian answer to the peace sign. One finger, pointed up.
scriptures: Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Mat 7:13
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Mat 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
corruption_summary: A faithful sign; its only danger is becoming a slogan without the life behind it, and its offense — one way — is the offense of the gospel itself.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in the One Way sign itself; it says what Scripture says. The danger with any Christian slogan is that it can become a badge of a subculture rather than a confession of faith — a sticker on the bumper while the driver cuts people off. The Jesus Movement produced a great deal of Christian merchandise, and later generations have produced much more. The sign is only as true as the life that holds it up.

The offense of the sign is unavoidable. The 1960s taught that every path is valid and that claiming one way is intolerant. The gospel cannot accept that, because it is not a philosophy among others but a rescue by a particular Person at a particular cross. The narrow way is narrow because it is a Person (Joh 14:6), and the gate is open to everyone who will come.
roots_summary: Old English án (one) + weg (way) → traffic sign one way → early-1970s Jesus Movement sign (raised index finger).
roots_lines: Old English weg — a way, a road, a course (see Way)
20th c.: one-way traffic signs
Early 1970s: the One Way sign of the Jesus Movement
June 1972: Explo ’72, Dallas — crowds raise the One Way sign
Greek hodos — way, road; "I am the way" (Joh 14:6)
usage: "Grandma still raises one finger instead of two in photos. She says it’s the One Way sign, from 1972."
I am the way, the truth, and the life (Joh 14:6).
This is the way, walk ye in it (Isa 30:21).

etymology: The signature farewell of Adam Clayton Powell Jr. (1908–1972), pastor of Harlem’s Abyssinian Baptist Church and U.S. congressman, who used it as a rallying cry, especially in 1967 when the House voted to exclude him amid charges of misusing funds (the Supreme Court later ruled the exclusion unconstitutional, Powell v. McCormack, 1969); his book of sermons was titled Keep the Faith, Baby! (1967). The phrase passed into general use as an upbeat "hang in there." It echoes Paul’s "I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7).
biblical_def: Keep the faith, baby was Adam Clayton Powell’s sign-off, and it became a 1960s and 70s way to say "hang in there, stay strong, don’t give up." The Christian observation: the slogan borrows one of the most important phrases in the New Testament and usually empties it. When Paul wrote, at the end of his life, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7), he did not mean that he had stayed optimistic. He meant he had guarded a definite body of truth — "the faith which was once delivered unto the saints," for which Jude tells believers to "earnestly contend" (Jud 1:3) — and had trusted the Person it reveals, through beatings, shipwreck, and prison. To keep the faith in that sense is to hold the gospel without adding to it or subtracting from it, and to keep trusting Christ until death. "Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)" (Heb 10:23). "Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life" (Rev 2:10). Powell himself was a complicated man, a gifted preacher whose public life was marked by scandal, and the slogan’s easy cheerfulness sits beside a hard question every believer must face: what faith am I keeping? A father can say "keep the faith" to his son as a blessing, and mean by it exactly what Paul meant.
webster_summary: Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s 1960s catchphrase (book, 1967) for "hang in there" — a borrowing of Paul’s "I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7), which means guarding the faith once delivered (Jud 1:3) and trusting Christ unto death.
webster_full: KEEP THE FAITH, BABY, catchphrase (1960s; Adam Clayton Powell Jr.) Stay strong; do not give up; remain loyal to the cause. Also simply keep the faith, as a farewell.

Webster (1828) — FAITH, noun [Latin fides, fido, to trust; Gr. to persuade, to draw towards any thing, to conciliate; to believe, to obey. In the Greek Lexicon of Hederic it is said, the primitive signification of the verb is to bind and draw or lead, as signifies a rope or cable. But this remark is a little incorrect. The sense of the verb, from which that of rope and binding is derived, is to strain, to draw, and thus to bind or make fast. A rope or cable is that which makes fast. Heb.] 1. Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity, without other evidence; the judgment that what another states or testifies is the truth. I have strong faith or no faith in the testimony of a witness, or in what a historian narrates. 2. The assent of the mind to the truth of a proposition advanced by another; belief, or probable evidence of any kind. 3.
Decode for families: in the New Testament, the faith is a definite body of truth (Jud 1:3) as well as trust in Christ. Keep both.
scriptures: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
corruption_summary: The catchphrase turned Paul’s confession into a cheerful "hang in there"; Scripture means by keeping the faith a lifelong guarding of revealed truth and trust in Christ unto death.
corruption_paragraphs: Slogans often steal from Scripture, and this one stole a precious phrase. Keep the faith became a way to encourage persistence in any cause — political, personal, athletic — with no particular faith in view. That flattening matches the culture’s view of faith as a feeling of confidence rather than trust in a revealed truth. A man can "keep the faith" in that sense while abandoning every doctrine of the Christian faith.

Paul’s words in 2Ti 4:7 were written from a Roman cell, shortly before his execution. They are a soldier’s report at the end of a campaign: the fight fought, the race run, the deposit guarded. A Christian family can reclaim the phrase by filling it again: the faith of the Apostles’ Creed, the faith of the catechism, the faith in Christ crucified and risen. Keep that faith, and the crown of life (Rev 2:10) is promised.
roots_summary: Latin fides → Old French feid → English faith; Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s catchphrase (1960s; book 1967) echoing 2Ti 4:7.
roots_lines: Latin fides — trust, confidence, loyalty; Greek pistis — faith, trust; the faith
2Ti 4:7 — "I have kept the faith" (tēn pistin tetērēka)
Adam Clayton Powell Jr. (1908–1972): Abyssinian Baptist Church; U.S. House, 1945–71
1967: Keep the Faith, Baby! (book); the House excludes Powell
1969: Powell v. McCormack — the Supreme Court rules the exclusion unconstitutional
usage: "Grandpa signs every birthday card ‘Keep the faith.’ He means 2 Timothy 4:7, and he says so."
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith (2Ti 4:7).
Earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints (Jud 1:3).

etymology: African-American colloquial of the 1960s, meaning to speak frankly and truthfully without softening, popularized by the civil-rights movement and by Aaron Neville’s hit "Tell It Like It Is" (late 1966, No. 2 pop, No. 1 R&B). By 1968 it was a general expression of praise for blunt honesty, used by everyone from preachers to sportscasters (Howard Cosell made it his motto).
biblical_def: To tell it like it is is to speak plainly and honestly, without spin or sugarcoating — and in the 1960s it was high praise, the opposite of the establishment’s smooth evasions. The Christian observation: Scripture loves plain truth-telling and gives it two partners the slogan sometimes forgets. First, truth itself: "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another" (Eph 4:25). The prophets told it like it was to kings. Nathan stood before David, who had committed adultery and murder, and said, "Thou art the man" (2Sa 12:7). Paul asked the Galatians, "Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?" (Gal 4:16). "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6). Second, love: "speaking the truth in love" (Eph 4:15). Telling it like it is can become an excuse for cruelty — "I’m just being honest" — and Scripture does not bless honesty that wounds for the pleasure of wounding. Third, grace: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man" (Col 4:6). Nathan told David the truth by telling him a story first, and he did it to bring him to repentance, not to win an argument. A father who tells his son the truth plainly, lovingly, and at the right time is telling it like it is in the biblical sense.
webster_summary: 1960s AAVE phrase (Aaron Neville hit, 1966) for speaking frankly without softening — a truth-telling Scripture commends (Eph 4:25; 2Sa 12:7) when it is joined to love (Eph 4:15) and grace (Col 4:6).
webster_full: TELL IT LIKE IT IS, phr. (1960s; Boomer era) To speak frankly and honestly; to describe a situation truthfully without euphemism or evasion. "At least he tells it like it is."

Webster (1828) — TELL, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive told. [Latin telum; Latin appello and peal, Latin pello.] 1. To utter; to express in words; to communicate to others. I will not eat till I have told my errand. Genesis 24:23 . 2. To relate; to narrate; to rehearse particulars; as, to tell a story. Genesis 37:16 . And not a man appears to tell their fate. 3. To teach; to inform; to make known; to show by words. tell us the way. Why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife? Gen 12.
Decode for families: "keeping it real" and "no filter" are its descendants. Ask whether love is in the room too.
scriptures: Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Eph 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;
Gal 4:16
Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: The phrase rightly praises plain truth over evasion but can excuse cruelty as honesty; Scripture demands truth spoken in love and seasoned with grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1960s were sick of euphemism — the government’s word games about Vietnam, the smooth lies of advertising, the silence of churches about segregation. Tell it like it is was a cry for honesty, and it was often a righteous one. Scripture has always demanded it; the prophets were the original truth-tellers, and they paid for it.

But a culture that prizes bluntness for its own sake slides toward brutality. "I’m just telling it like it is" becomes the excuse for every cruel word. Eph 4:15 holds the two together: truth and love are not rivals but partners. The truth without love is a club; love without truth is a lie. Nathan’s parable is the model — perfect honesty, delivered with wisdom, aimed at the sinner’s restoration.
roots_summary: Old English tellan (to count, to relate) → tell; 1960s AAVE tell it like it is → Aaron Neville, 1966 → general praise for frankness.
roots_lines: Old English tellan — to count, to reckon, to relate (see Tell)
1960s African-American colloquial: tell it like it is — speak the plain truth
Late 1966: Aaron Neville, "Tell It Like It Is"
Late 1960s: general use; sportscaster Howard Cosell’s motto
Greek alētheuō — to speak the truth (Eph 4:15)
usage: "Grandma tells it like it is. She also bakes you cookies afterward. That’s Ephesians 4:15."
Speaking the truth in love (Eph 4:15).
Thou art the man (2Sa 12:7).

etymology: From a vaudeville and "chitlin circuit" comedy routine performed for decades by Dewey "Pigmeat" Markham, who entered as a bombastic judge to the chant "Here come de judge!" The routine reached a national audience in 1968 on NBC’s Rowan & Martin’s Laugh-In, first with Sammy Davis Jr. in robe and wig, then with Markham himself, and Markham’s novelty record "Here Comes the Judge" (1968) became a hit. For a year or two everyone said it.
biblical_def: Here come da judge! was the 1968 catchphrase from Laugh-In: a comic judge in an oversized robe swaggering in to dispense absurd justice, and everyone in America repeating the line. The Christian observation: the joke works because it plays with something every person knows to be serious — the arrival of a judge. Scripture says that arrival is coming for real, and it is no joke. "Behold, the judge standeth before the door" (Jas 5:9). God "hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead" (Act 17:31). That Man is Christ, for "the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" (Joh 5:22), and "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ" (2Co 5:10). Unlike the comic judge, this Judge is perfectly just; Abraham asked the question that settles every doubt: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" (Gen 18:25). The glorious twist of the gospel is that the coming Judge is also the Savior who bore the judgment for those who trust Him. A family can laugh at Pigmeat Markham, and then tell the children that the real Judge is coming — and that He is the best friend a guilty sinner could have, if they come to Him before the court convenes.
webster_summary: 1968 catchphrase (Pigmeat Markham’s routine; Laugh-In) for a comic judge’s entrance — a joke that plays on the real coming Judge, Christ, who will judge the world in righteousness (Act 17:31) and is the Savior of all who trust Him.
webster_full: HERE COME DA JUDGE, catchphrase (1968; Boomer era TV) The announcement of a comic judge’s entrance, from Pigmeat Markham’s routine as revived on Rowan & Martin’s Laugh-In; used humorously of anyone arriving with authority. Also Here comes the judge.

Webster (1828) — JUDGE, noun [Latin judex, supposed to be compounded of jus, law or right, and dico, to pronounce.] 1. A civil officer who is invested with authority to hear and determine causes, civil or criminal, between parties, according to his commission; as the judges of the king’s bench, or of the common pleas; judges of the supreme court, of district courts, or of a county court. The judge of a court of equity is called a chancellor. 2. The Supreme Being. Shall not the judge of all the earth do right? Genesis 18:25 . 3. One who presides in a court of judicature.
Decode for families: the comic judge is a parody. The real one is not (2Co 5:10).
scriptures: Jas 5:9
Grudge not one against another, brethren, lest ye be condemned: behold, the judge standeth before the door.

Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead.
Joh 5:22
For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son:
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.

That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?
corruption_summary: A harmless comic routine; its echo is the most serious truth in the world — the Judge is coming — and the gospel’s surprise that the Judge is also the Savior.
corruption_paragraphs: Comedy about judges is as old as courts, and Pigmeat Markham’s routine was cheerful slapstick. Nothing in it needs rebuke. But a culture that knows judges mainly as punchlines may find it hard to take the Last Judgment seriously, and Scripture insists on it. "Here comes the judge" is, in fact, the message of the whole New Testament: the Judge is standing at the door (Jas 5:9).

The gospel turns the joke inside out. The Judge who is coming has already come once, not to judge but to be judged — condemned in a Roman court, executed, and raised. Those who belong to Him will stand in the judgment clothed in His righteousness. Gen 18:25 is the believer’s comfort: the Judge of all the earth will do right, and He has already done right by His people at the cross.
roots_summary: Latin iudex (judge) → Old French juge → English judge; Pigmeat Markham’s vaudeville routine → 1968 Laugh-In revival and hit record.
roots_lines: Latin ius (law) + dicere (to say) → iudex — one who declares the law
Dewey "Pigmeat" Markham (1904–1981): the "Here come de judge" routine on the vaudeville circuit
1968: Rowan & Martin’s Laugh-In (NBC) — Sammy Davis Jr., then Markham
1968: "Here Comes the Judge" novelty record
Greek kritēs — judge; bēma — judgment seat (2Co 5:10)
usage: "When Grandpa walks into the kitchen to referee an argument, Grandma says, ‘Here come da judge.’"
Behold, the judge standeth before the door (Jas 5:9).
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? (Gen 18:25).

etymology: From a Wendy’s hamburger commercial first aired in January 1984, in which the 81-year-old actress Clara Peller peers at a rival’s huge bun and tiny patty and demands, "Where’s the beef?" It became an instant catchphrase, and in a March 1984 primary debate Walter Mondale turned it on Gary Hart’s "new ideas," making it shorthand for "Where is the substance?"
biblical_def: Where’s the beef? asks where the substance is behind the packaging — the meat in the bun, the content in the promise, the facts behind the slogan. Clara Peller asked it about a hamburger in 1984, and Walter Mondale asked it about a rival’s campaign. The Christian observation: it is one of the most biblical questions in the advertising history of the Boomer era. Scripture asks it constantly. James asks it of faith: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone" (Jas 2:17). Paul asks it of religion: there are those "Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away" (2Ti 3:5). The Lord Jesus gives the test: "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them" (Mat 7:20). And the writer to the Hebrews asks it of spiritual growth, using a food image of his own: believers who should be mature "are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat. ... But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil" (Heb 5:12, 14). A church with a big bun and a small patty — impressive building, clever programs, thin preaching — deserves Clara Peller’s question. So does a Christian life with a big profession and little obedience. A father can ask it of himself first, and then teach his children to ask it of every slogan, sermon, and sales pitch they hear.
webster_summary: 1984 Wendy’s catchphrase (Clara Peller), turned political by Walter Mondale, demanding substance behind packaging — the question Scripture asks of faith without works (Jas 2:17) and a form of godliness without power (2Ti 3:5).
webster_full: WHERE’S THE BEEF?, catchphrase (1984; Boomer era) Where is the substance? Used to challenge something that looks impressive but lacks content. From a Wendy’s commercial (January 1984); used by Walter Mondale against Gary Hart (March 1984).

Webster (1828) — BEEF, noun [Latin bos, bovis; Gr.Bous.] 1. An animal of the bovine genus, whether ox, bull or cow; but used of those which are full grown or nearly so. In this, which is the original sense, the word has a plural, beeves. 2. The flesh of an ox, bull, or cow, when killed. In popular language, the word is often applied to the live animal; as, an ox is good beef; that is, is well fattened. In this sense, the word has no plural.
Decode for families: the modern version is "all hat, no cattle," or "where are the receipts?"
scriptures: Jas 2:17
Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
Mat 7:20
Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
Heb 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
corruption_summary: A fair and useful question from a hamburger ad; Scripture asks it of every profession of faith, every form of godliness, and every church fed on milk when it should be eating strong meat.
corruption_paragraphs: The irony of the slogan is that it was itself advertising — packaging about packaging — and it worked because everyone recognized the con it was mocking. The 1980s were an age of image: politics by commercial, products sold by lifestyle, and a growing evangelical media world that could also be all bun. The question cut through, and it still does.

Scripture’s version is searching rather than sarcastic. James is not mocking weak believers; he is warning them that a faith that never feeds anyone is not living faith (Jas 2:17). Hebrews is not scolding beginners; it is calling them to grow up into strong meat (Heb 5:14). The church that answers "Where’s the beef?" with the whole counsel of God, faithfully preached and lived, has nothing to fear from the question.
roots_summary: Old French boef (ox) → English beef → January 1984 Wendy’s ad (Clara Peller) → March 1984 Mondale debate → general "Where’s the substance?"
roots_lines: Latin bos, bovis — ox → Old French boef → English beef
January 1984: Wendy’s "Where’s the beef?" commercial with Clara Peller
March 1984: Walter Mondale uses it against Gary Hart in a Democratic primary debate
Separate slang: beef — a complaint or grudge ("what’s your beef?")
Greek sterea trophē — "strong meat," solid food (Heb 5:12–14)
usage: "Grandpa listened to the candidate for ten minutes and asked, ‘Where’s the beef?’ Grandma laughed so hard she had to sit down."
Faith, if it hath not works, is dead (Jas 2:17).
Strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age (Heb 5:14).

etymology: Shortened from square business, African-American slang of the 1960s–70s for the honest truth, serious matters, or straight dealing ("I’m telling you square business"), from square in its old sense of fair, honest, exact (a square deal, fair and square; Webster 1828: "That does equal justice; exact; fair; honest; as square dealing"). Teena Marie’s funk hit "Square Biz" (1981) made the short form famous.
biblical_def: Square biz means straight talk and honest dealing — "no jive, this is square business." It uses square not in the hippie sense of "uncool" but in the older sense of fair and true, the sense in a square deal and fair and square. The Christian observation: the phrase lands on one of the most practical virtues in Scripture — honesty in business. God cares about the scale in the marketplace: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Pro 11:1). "Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt" (Lev 19:36) — honesty in trade is grounded in redemption. The man who may dwell in God’s holy hill is "He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart" (Psa 15:2). Paul handled money for the churches carefully: "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men" (2Co 8:21). In a culture of hustles, scams, and spin, a Christian whose word is square business is a witness. A father in business can teach his son that the square deal is not a weakness but a confession of faith in the God who sees the scales.
webster_summary: 1960s–70s AAVE slang (square business; Teena Marie, 1981) for honest truth and straight dealing — on the 1828 square, "honest, fair" — the just weight that is the LORD’s delight (Pro 11:1).
webster_full: SQUARE BIZ, n. (AAVE, 1960s–70s; Boomer era) Honest truth; serious, legitimate business; straight dealing. From square business. "That’s square biz."
Webster (1828) — SQUARE, adjective 5. That does equal justice; exact; fair; honest; as square dealing.
Note the two Boomer squares: the hippie’s square (conventional, uncool — see Square) and the street’s square biz (honest). The second is the older and better one.
scriptures: Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.
Psa 15:2
He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.
Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
corruption_summary: A wholesome phrase prizing honesty; Scripture grounds the square deal in the God who delights in a just weight and redeemed His people to live honestly.
corruption_paragraphs: Square biz needs no correction; it names a virtue. Its value is the contrast it draws with its own neighborhood of slang — jive, hustle, con, game — all words for dishonest talk and dealing. A community that has been cheated prizes a word for the honest man, and Scripture prizes him too.

The deeper point is that Scripture roots business honesty in theology. Lev 19:36 ties just weights to the Exodus: the God who freed you from Egypt’s cheating masters will not have you cheat your neighbors. A Christian businessman who keeps square accounts is not merely being prudent; he is confessing that he serves a God who sees every scale.
roots_summary: Latin exquadrare (to make square) → Old French esquare → English square (exact; honest, fair) + business → 1960s–70s AAVE square business → 1981 "Square Biz."
roots_lines: Latin ex + quadrare — to make square, to make exact
English square — true, exact; honest, fair (a square deal, fair and square)
1960s–70s AAVE: square business — the honest truth; legitimate dealing
1981: Teena Marie, "Square Biz"
Hebrew eben shelemah — "a just weight," literally a whole stone (Pro 11:1)
usage: "When Grandpa sold me his old truck, he said, ‘Square biz — the transmission slips in the rain.’ That’s why I trust him."
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight (Pro 11:1).
Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men (2Co 8:21).

etymology: A 1970s African-American greeting, "What it is!" (often answered "What it was!" or "What it is, brother!"), roughly "Hello, what’s happening?", carried into general slang by television and film of the decade. The fuller "It is what it is" (resigned acceptance) is a separate, later expression that became common in the 2000s.
biblical_def: What it is! was a 1970s greeting — a cool way to say hello and "what’s going on?" at once. Two friends meet on the street: "What it is!" "What it is, man." The Christian observation: a greeting is a small thing that Scripture takes seriously, because a greeting can carry a blessing. When Boaz walked into his barley field, he greeted his workers, "The LORD be with you," and they answered him, "The LORD bless thee" (Rut 2:4). That is a greeting with God in it. The priests of Israel greeted the people with the great benediction: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace" (Num 6:24–26). The Psalmist mourns the passersby who never say, "The blessing of the LORD be upon you" (Psa 129:8). John opens a letter, "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (3Jn 1:2). The modern greeting has shrunk to "hey" and "what’s up," and the old 1970s "what it is" was at least warm. A Christian can be warmer still. "A word spoken in due season, how good is it!" (Pro 15:23). A father who greets his children in the morning with a blessing is doing what Boaz did in the field.
webster_summary: 1970s AAVE greeting ("What it is!"), roughly "Hello, what’s happening?" — a warm hello Scripture can fill with blessing, as Boaz greeted his reapers: "The LORD be with you" (Rut 2:4).
webster_full: WHAT IT IS, interj. (AAVE, 1970s; Boomer era) A greeting: hello; what’s happening? Reply often "What it is!" or "What it was!"
Distinct from it is what it is (2000s), an expression of resigned acceptance.
Decode for families: greetings matter. Teach your children one with a blessing in it.
scriptures: Rut 2:4
And, behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said unto the reapers, The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee.
Num 6:24
The LORD bless thee, and keep thee:
Num 6:25
The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee:
Num 6:26
The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
Neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the LORD be upon you: we bless you in the name of the LORD.
Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth.
corruption_summary: A harmless and friendly greeting; Scripture shows how much more a greeting can carry when it brings the blessing of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in what it is; it is a friendly hello. The modern cousin, it is what it is, deserves a gentler critique: it is a shrug of fatalism, the language of a world without providence. The Christian never quite says "it is what it is," because he knows Who governs what is and that all things work together for good to them that love God.

The positive lesson is Ruth 2:4. In a farm field in Bethlehem, a landowner and his workers greeted each other in the name of the LORD, and the whole book of Ruth unfolds from that field of mutual blessing. A family that greets one another, and its neighbors, with a word of blessing is practicing a lost art that the Bible treats as worship.
roots_summary: 1970s AAVE greeting What it is! (reply What it was!); distinct from 2000s it is what it is.

usage: "Grandpa walked into the barbershop and said, ‘What it is!’ The barber said, ‘What it was!’ They’ve been friends since 1974."
The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee (Rut 2:4).
The LORD bless thee, and keep thee (Num 6:24).

etymology: From astrology: the slow precession of the equinoxes moves the sun’s position at the spring equinox backward through the zodiac, roughly one sign every two thousand years, and astrologers taught that the "Age of Pisces" was ending and the "Age of Aquarius" — an era of harmony, brotherhood, and spiritual awakening — was dawning. The phrase was popularized by the rock musical Hair (off-Broadway 1967, Broadway 1968), whose opening song "Aquarius" proclaimed it, and by the 5th Dimension’s medley "Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In" (No. 1, 1969). It became a byword for the New Age movement.
biblical_def: The Age of Aquarius was the hippie’s promised new era: an astrological age of peace, love, harmony, and spiritual enlightenment that was supposedly dawning in the late 1960s, announced by the musical Hair and sung on every radio in 1969. The Christian observation: the phrase is astrology dressed as hope, and Scripture is plain about both. Of astrology, the prophet mocks Babylon’s reliance on it: "Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee. Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them" (Isa 47:13–14). "Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them" (Jer 10:2). Israel was forbidden any "observer of times" (Deu 18:10). The stars do not govern history; they declare their Maker: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psa 19:1). Of hope, Scripture says a new age has indeed dawned, but not by the movement of constellations. The only star that ever announced an age pointed the wise men to a manger: "we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him" (Mat 2:2). The age of harmony and brotherhood the song longed for is the kingdom of Christ, begun at His first coming and consummated at His second. The Age of Aquarius did not arrive in 1969; the kingdom of God arrived in Bethlehem, and it is still advancing.
webster_summary: Astrological "new age" of harmony said to be dawning in the late 1960s, popularized by Hair (1967–68) and "Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In" (1969) — astrology Scripture forbids (Isa 47:13–14; Deu 18:10), set against the star that led to Christ (Mat 2:2).
webster_full: AGE OF AQUARIUS, n. (astrological; Boomer-era popularization 1967–69) In astrology, an era of about two thousand years associated with the sign Aquarius, believed by its proponents to bring peace, harmony, and spiritual awakening; hence the New Age hopes of the 1960s counterculture.

Webster (1828) — AQUARIUS, noun [Latin] The water bearer; a sign in the zodiac which the sun enters about the 21st day of January; so called from the rains which prevail at that season, in Italy and the East. The stars in this constellation according to Ptolenty, are 45; according to Tycho Brahe, 41; according to Hevelius, 45; and according to Flamstead, 108.
Decode for families: horoscopes, zodiac apps, and "what’s your sign?" are the Age of Aquarius still on the shelf. Teach Psa 19:1.
scriptures: Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee.
Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them; they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame: there shall not be a coal to warm at, nor fire to sit before it.
Jer 10:2
Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them.
There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Mat 2:2
Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.
corruption_summary: The Age of Aquarius promised a new era of harmony governed by the stars; Scripture forbids astrology, makes the stars heralds of God’s glory, and locates the new age in the kingdom of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Hair was a musical about draft resistance, drugs, and free love, and its opening anthem baptized all of it in astrology. The counterculture’s turn to the stars was part of a larger turn from the church to every alternative religion available — tarot, the I Ching, Eastern mysticism, the occult. That turn did not fade with the 1960s; it became the New Age movement and lives on in the horoscope apps of today. Scripture’s verdict has not changed: the astrologers cannot save (Isa 47:13), and God’s people are not to be dismayed at the signs of heaven (Jer 10:2).

There is a better reading of the sky. The heavens declare God’s glory (Psa 19:1), and once a star led seekers from the East to the true King (Mat 2:2). The wise men left their astrology at the manger and worshiped. Every seeker who has looked to the stars for meaning can be invited to do the same.
roots_summary: Latin Aquarius (water-bearer) → zodiac sign → astrological "Age of Aquarius" (precession of the equinoxes) → Hair (1967–68) → 1969 No. 1 hit → New Age movement.

1969: the 5th Dimension, "Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In," No. 1

usage: "Grandma sang ‘Aquarius’ at her high school talent show in 1969. She sang ‘Joy to the World’ at church that Christmas and says she meant that one more."
Be not dismayed at the signs of heaven (Jer 10:2).
We have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him (Mat 2:2).

etymology: Coined by Jack Weinberg, a leader of the Free Speech Movement at the University of California, Berkeley, in an interview with a San Francisco Chronicle reporter in November 1964; Weinberg later said he meant it as a jab at the idea that the students were being manipulated by older outside agitators. It became one of the defining slogans of the 1960s generation gap.
biblical_def: Don’t trust anyone over 30 was the student slogan of the mid-1960s: the older generation — parents, professors, politicians — had made a mess of the world and could not be trusted; the young would do better. Every Boomer who said it turned thirty within a decade or so. The Christian observation: the slogan reverses Scripture’s counsel, and Scripture shows where that reversal leads. When Rehoboam became king of Israel, the old men who had served his father Solomon advised him to lighten the people’s yoke. "But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him" (1Ki 12:8), and the kingdom split in two. Scripture’s ordinary rule is respect for age: "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding" (Job 12:12); "ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder" (1Pe 5:5). Yet Scripture is not naive about the old either. Young Elihu said, "Great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment" (Job 32:9), and Paul told Timothy, "Let no man despise thy youth" (1Ti 4:12). The Bible’s answer is not to trust the old or the young as a class but to trust God and weigh every man’s counsel by His Word: "It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man" (Psa 118:8). The grandparent who once chanted this slogan is now over thirty twice; he may be the best person to explain why it was wrong.
webster_summary: Free Speech Movement slogan (Jack Weinberg, Berkeley, November 1964) for distrusting the older generation — the counsel of Rehoboam’s young men (1Ki 12:8), set against Scripture’s respect for age (Job 12:12) and its higher rule: trust in the LORD (Psa 118:8).
webster_full: DON’T TRUST ANYONE OVER 30, slogan (1964; Boomer era) The 1960s youth movement’s expression of distrust toward the older generation and its institutions. Attributed to Jack Weinberg of the Berkeley Free Speech Movement.

Webster (1828) — TRUST, noun 1. Confidence; a reliance or resting of the mind on the integrity, veracity, justice, friendship or other sound principle of another person. He that putteth his trust in the Lord shall be safe. Proverbs 29:25 . 2. He or that which is the ground of confidence. O Lord God, thou art my trust from my youth. Psalms 71:1 . 3. Charge received in confidence. Reward them well, if they observe their trust
Decode for families: every generation has its version. The Boomers who said it are now the elders their grandchildren are tempted to ignore.
scriptures: But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him, and which stood before him:
With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
Job 32:9
Great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man.
corruption_summary: The slogan made age itself a reason for distrust; Scripture honors the wisdom of age, refuses to idolize either young or old, and teaches trust in the LORD above all.
corruption_paragraphs: The slogan expressed something real: the young of 1964 had watched their elders build a segregated South and a nuclear arms race, and they had reasons for suspicion. But it hardened a reasonable suspicion into a rule, and the rule cut the young off from the wisdom they most needed. Rehoboam’s story (1Ki 12) is the biblical case study. The advice of his peers sounded bold; it was folly, and the nation paid.

Scripture’s balance is wiser than either the slogan or its opposite. Age deserves honor (Job 12:12; 1Pe 5:5), but not blind trust (Job 32:9). Youth deserves respect (1Ti 4:12), but not autonomy. The final authority is neither generation but God (Psa 118:8). A family where grandparents, parents, and children all sit under the same Word has found the cure for the generation gap that the slogan made worse.
roots_summary: Jack Weinberg, Berkeley Free Speech Movement, November 1964 (San Francisco Chronicle) → national slogan of the 1960s generation gap.

Later 1960s: a byword of the generation gap
Hebrew zeqenim — the old men, elders (1Ki 12:8)
usage: "Grandpa said it in 1966. He turned thirty in 1975 and, he says, became trustworthy that very afternoon."

It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man (Psa 118:8).

etymology: Usually traced to October 2, 1977, at Dodger Stadium, when Los Angeles outfielder Glenn Burke raised his hand overhead to greet teammate Dusty Baker after Baker’s 30th home run of the season, and Baker slapped it; college basketball players at Louisville popularized the gesture in 1978–79, and the phrase high five is recorded by 1980. It grew from the older low-hand slap, give me five / give me some skin.
biblical_def: A high five is the raised-palm slap of celebration: a home run, a good grade, a finished job. It was born, as far as anyone can tell, in a Dodgers dugout in 1977 and became universal within a few years. The Christian observation: the gesture is a small act of shared joy, and Scripture loves shared joy. "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15) — a high five is the first half of that verse in a single motion. The Psalms command the whole body in praise: "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph" (Psa 47:1). And when the apostles recognized God’s grace on Paul, they gave him and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship" (Gal 2:9), a public sign of partnership in the gospel. The high five belongs to the same family: a hand raised to say "we’re in this together, and this is good." Scripture asks believers to be generous with that kind of encouragement: "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1Th 5:11); "let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works" (Heb 10:24). A father who high-fives his son for telling the truth when it cost him something is doing more than celebrating; he is teaching what is worth celebrating.
webster_summary: Celebratory raised-palm slap traced to the Dodgers’ Glenn Burke and Dusty Baker (October 2, 1977), named by 1980 — a gesture of shared joy Scripture commends: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice" (Rom 12:15).
webster_full: HIGH FIVE, n. (late 1970s; named by 1980) A gesture of celebration or greeting in which two people slap raised palms together. v.t. To give someone a high five. Compare low five, give me five, give me some skin.
Decode for families: the most cheerful thing the late Boomer years gave the world.
scriptures: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Psa 47:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah. O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph.
Gal 2:9

And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.
Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
corruption_summary: A wholesome gesture of shared joy; its only lesson is to celebrate what is truly good and to be quick to encourage one another.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in the high five needs correction. If there is a caution, it is about what we celebrate. A culture high-fives touchdowns and paychecks; a Christian family can add honesty, kindness, and faithfulness to the list. Children learn what their parents value by what their parents celebrate.

The gesture also models something the church needs: visible encouragement. Hebrews tells believers to "provoke" one another to love and good works (Heb 10:24) — to stir each other up. A congregation that celebrates a teenager’s profession of faith, a couple’s fiftieth anniversary, or a new believer’s baptism with the joy of a dugout after a home run is practicing Rom 12:15.
roots_summary: Give me five / give me some skin (low hand slap, mid-20th c.) → October 2, 1977, Burke and Baker → 1978–79 Louisville basketball → high five, by 1980.

October 2, 1977: Glenn Burke and Dusty Baker, Dodger Stadium
1978–79: Louisville Cardinals basketball players popularize it
By 1980: high five in print
Greek dexias koinōnias — "right hands of fellowship" (Gal 2:9)
usage: "Grandpa high-fived me when I memorized Romans 12. He missed and hit the lamp."
Rejoice with them that do rejoice (Rom 12:15).
They gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship (Gal 2:9).

etymology: Jazz and jive talk of the 1930s–40s: give me some skin or slip me some skin, a request for a friendly hand slap or handshake, palm against palm, as a greeting, congratulation, or seal of agreement. It passed into 1950s–60s Black and hipster slang, was used by Boomer teens, and gave rise to give me five, low five, and finally the high five of the late 1970s.
biblical_def: Gimme some skin means "slap my hand" — a hip handshake, palm sliding across palm, for hello, congratulations, or "it’s a deal." It is the ancestor of the high five. The Christian observation: Scripture knows the meaning of a hand given, and it knows both its warmth and its weight. The warmth: when Jehu met Jehonadab on the road, he asked, "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? And Jehonadab answered, It is. If it be, give me thine hand. And he gave him his hand" (2Ki 10:15). The apostles gave Paul "the right hands of fellowship" (Gal 2:9). A hand given is a heart pledged; that is why a handshake once meant more than a contract. The weight: Proverbs warns that striking hands can bind a man to another’s debts. "My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger" (Pro 6:1), deliver yourself; "Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts" (Pro 22:26). The slap of agreement is a promise, and promises bind. So a Christian can give some skin freely in greeting and joy, and carefully in business. And the deepest word about skin and hands in Scripture belongs to Christ, whose hands were pierced to seal the covenant that saves — "a friend loveth at all times" (Pro 17:17), and He is that Friend.
webster_summary: 1930s–40s jive talk, carried into Boomer slang, for a palm-slap handshake of greeting or agreement, ancestor of the high five — a hand given is a heart pledged (2Ki 10:15), and a hand struck can bind (Pro 6:1).
webster_full: GIMME SOME SKIN, phr. (jazz / jive slang, 1930s–40s; Boomer-era use) Give me a hand slap or handshake, as a greeting, congratulation, or sign of agreement. Also slip me some skin, give me five.

Webster (1828) — SKIN, noun 1. The natural covering of animal bodies, consisting of the cuticle or scarf-skin, the rete mucosum, and the cutis or hide. The cuticle is very thin and insensible; the cutis is thicker and very sensible. 2. A hide; a pelt; the skin of an animal separated from the body, whether green, dry or tanned.
Decode for families: before the high five there was skin. Before skin, there was the handshake that meant "my word is good."
scriptures: And when he was departed thence, he lighted on Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him: and he saluted him, and said to him, Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? And Jehonadab answered, It is. If it be, give me thine hand. And he gave him his hand; and he took him up to him into the chariot.
Gal 2:9

And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.
Pro 6:1
My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger,
Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
corruption_summary: A friendly, harmless gesture; Scripture adds that a hand given pledges the heart and that a hand struck in agreement can bind, so it should be given freely in friendship and carefully in debt.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing sinful in a hand slap, and the jive-era greeting carried a real warmth among friends who had little else to give each other. The only lesson Scripture adds is about the weight of the hand. In the ancient world, as in many places still, striking hands sealed an agreement, and Proverbs warns young men again and again not to strike hands as surety for others’ debts. A culture that has turned the handshake into a casual gesture may have lost the sense that a man’s word, sealed by his hand, should be good.

The warm side of the gesture is Jehu’s question: "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?" (2Ki 10:15). That is what every true greeting asks. A Christian who gives some skin to a brother is, in a small way, giving the right hand of fellowship (Gal 2:9).
roots_summary: Old Norse skinn (hide) → English skin; 1930s–40s jive give / slip me some skin → 1950s–60s give me five → late-1970s high five.
roots_lines: Old Norse skinn — skin, hide (see Skin)
1930s–40s jazz and jive talk: give me some skin, slip me some skin
1950s–60s: give me five, low five
Late 1970s: the high five
Hebrew taqa kaph — to strike hands, as surety (Pro 6:1; Pro 22:26)
usage: "Grandpa held out his palm and said, ‘Gimme some skin.’ My little brother just stared at him."
Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? ... give me thine hand (2Ki 10:15).
Be not thou one of them that strike hands (Pro 22:26).
